units.translation: which the scholiast explains as δάκρυε τὸ ἀτύχημα [weep for the misfortune]. But the question is how the metrical fault is to be removed, since synizesis cannot be considered, nor can ἴαιν᾽ ἴαινε [warm, warm] be written with Heimsoeth (p. 352496), because that verb is usually said of joyful, not sad, things. Therefore, if Aeschylus used the verb διαίνω [to wet, moisten], about which there can scarcely be doubt, since the chorus answers Xerxes διαίνομαι γοεδνὸς ὤν [I am wet with tears, being mournful] and at 1065 Xerxes again says διαίνου δ᾽ ὄσσε [wet your eyes], and the chorus at v. 258 αἰαῖ, διαίνεσθε, Πέρσαι τόδ᾽ ἄχος κλύοντες [alas, wet yourselves, Persians, hearing this grief], where the scholiast likewise explains it by δακρύετε [weep], nothing remains but to write δίαιν δίαινε [wet, wet]. That a similar apocope παῦ [stop] is used for παθε [suffer] is known from Photius p. 403, 4, whence in Aristophanes Knights 821 παῦ παῦ᾽ οὗτος [stop, stop, you] has been restored, where the manuscripts, with the meter violated, have παῦ᾽ οὑτοσί [stop, this fellow]. Moreover, it is self-evident that this apocope has a place only where the same verb is repeated. Thus Aeschylus and Aristophanes could rightly say δίαιν δίαινε [wet, wet] and παῦ παῦε [stop, stop], but they could not simply say δίαιν [wet] and παῦ [stop], which is not proven by the formula ἄλευ δᾶ [avoid, O earth], about which I have spoken s.v. ἀλεύω [to avoid].
